# Software Architecture and Microservice Workshop

*Building effective software efficiently*

## Starting point

This is the second part of the Software Architecture and Microservices workshop.
It builds upon the previous section.

## Modular Monolithic Architecture

Modular monolithic architecture is a way to improve on the code locality by
partitioning the application by domain. In other words, all classes that belong
to the catalogue functionality will go to the `demo.catalogue` package and the
cart functionality will go to the `demo.cart` package. Note that no technical
(or roles) packages are used. All classes related to the catalogue functionality
will go to the `demo.catalogue` package and anyone working on this feature, can
simply focus on this package and do not have to look at the other packages
unless they need to. The following diagram shows how our project will be
reorganised.

![Refactoring from layered to modular monolithic architecture style](./assets/images/Refactoring%20from%20layered%20to%20modular%20monolithic%20architecture%20style.png)

Let’s look at the classes we have and how these are organised.

```shell
tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 2 './src/main/java'
```

The `src` directory should have the following structure.

```
./src/main/java
└── demo
    ├── cart
    ├── catalogue
    ├── common
    └── Main.java

5 directories, 1 file
```

### Architecture Decision Records (ADR)

In this example, the same application is restructured using a modular monolith
approach. This decision is also documented as an Architectural Decision Record
(ADR). It is assumed that the layered monolith was the initial architectural
choice, and that adopting the modular monolith represents an improvement upon
that design.

> **What should be done with the initial ADR, in which we documented our decision to use a layered monolithic architecture?**
>
> ADRs are not fixed and can evolve over time. In cases such as this, the
> original ADR should be marked as superseded, and a new ADR should be created
> to reflect the revised decision. One of the advantages of using Markdown is
> that it allows us to easily link related ADRs for clear traceability.

The initial layered monolithic architecture style, defined in `ADR-005`, has now
been superseded by the new modular monolithic architecture style as outlined in
`ADR-006`. `ADR-005` should be updated to reflect this change.

Lastly, update the `README.md` file, which summarises all ADRs, to clearly
indicate that ADR-005 has been superseded by ADR-006.

### Test the application

Please note that this architectural change does not modify the underlying
business logic. The business logic remains exactly as it was, without any
alterations.

Build the application and run the tests

```shell
./mvnw clean verify
```

All tests should pass

```
...
[INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
[INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
...
```

Try the application with the new modular monolithic architecture style.

```shell
# Start the application in the background
java -jar './target/application-monolithic-modular-single-project-1.0.0.jar' > './target/modular-single-project-monolithic-architecture.log' 2>&1 &

# Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
echo "$!" > './target/application-monolithic-modular-single-project.pid'

# Wait for the application to start
while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/cart/1')" -ne '200' ]; do echo 'Waiting for the application to start'; sleep 1; done
```

This starts our application in the background and waits until it is ready to
handle requests. The application is now running on localhost and listening on
port `8080`.

Make a few requests to the catalogue items endpoint. We have the following
catalogue items in the database.

| `id` | `caption`     | `description`                                                         |
| ---: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|    1 | Leather Sofa  | A very nice and comfortable sofa                                      |
|    2 | Wooden Table  | A large table ideal for 6 to 8 people                                 |
|    3 | Plastic Chair | A robust plastic chair ideal for children and adults alike            |
|    4 | Mug           | The ideal way to start the day                                        |
|    5 | LED TV        | A very large TV set, ideal for those who love to binge-watch TV shows |

Request the details for the item with id `2`.

```shell
curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/2' | jq
```

The catalogue item with id `2`

```json
{
  "id": 2,
  "caption": "Wooden Table",
  "description": "A large table ideal for 6 to 8 people"
}
```

Add a new item to the catalogue.

We will add a new item named `Green Plant`, with the description:
`Put a little life in your living room!`. The response will then be saved to a
file so that we can use the generated id to retrieve the item later.

```shell
# Save the response in a file as we will use it later on
curl --silent \
  -X POST 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"caption":"Green Plant","description":"Put a little life in your living room!!"}' \
  | jq \
  > new-catalogue-item.json

# Print the output
jq . new-catalogue-item.json
```

The newly added item

```json
{
  "id": 6,
  "caption": "Green Plant",
  "description": "Put a little life in your living room!!"
}
```

Fetch this item using the generated id.

```shell
# Read the new item id obtained from the previous command
ITEM_ID="$(jq .id new-catalogue-item.json)"

# Fetch the new item
curl --silent "http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/${ITEM_ID}" | jq
```

The newly added item

```json
{
  "id": 6,
  "caption": "Green Plant",
  "description": "Put a little life in your living room!!"
}
```

The database has three carts, as shown in the following table.

| `cart_id` | `item_id` | `caption`     | `quantity` |
| --------: | --------: | ------------- | ---------: |
|         1 |         1 | Leather Sofa  |          1 |
|         1 |         5 | LED TV        |          1 |
|         2 |         2 | Wooden Table  |          1 |
|         2 |         3 | Plastic Chair |          6 |
|         3 |         4 | Mug           |          4 |

Request the details for the cart with id `2`.

```shell
curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/cart/2' | jq
```

The cart with id `2` and its items

```json
{
  "id": 2,
  "items": [
    {
      "id": 2,
      "caption": "Wooden Table",
      "quantity": 1
    },
    {
      "id": 3,
      "caption": "Plastic Chair",
      "quantity": 6
    }
  ]
}
```

Add the new item to the cart.

```shell
# Read the new item id obtained from the previous command
ITEM_ID="$(jq .id new-catalogue-item.json)"

# Add the new item to cart with id 2
curl --silent -X POST "http://localhost:8080/cart/2/item/${ITEM_ID}" | jq
```

The cart contents after adding the newly created catalogue item.

```json
{
  "id": 2,
  "items": [
    {
      "id": 2,
      "caption": "Wooden Table",
      "quantity": 1
    },
    {
      "id": 3,
      "caption": "Plastic Chair",
      "quantity": 6
    },
    {
      "id": 6,
      "caption": "Green Plant",
      "quantity": 1
    }
  ]
}
```

Delete the temporary file `new-catalogue-item.json`, which was created to store
the id of the newly added item to the catalogue.

```shell
rm -rf new-catalogue-item.json
```

Stop the application once ready.

```shell
kill "$(cat './target/application-monolithic-modular-single-project.pid')"
rm -f './target/application-monolithic-modular-single-project.pid'
```

### Containers

As with the previous architectural approach, this JAR file may be packaged
within a container. In this example, we will use `jlink`, assuming the JAR file
has already been generated. For a full reference implementation, see
[`./containers/Dockerfile`](./containers/Dockerfile). Once completed, you can
build the container using this optimised method.

```shell
docker build \
  --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
  --tag 'demo:application-monolithic-modular-single-project' \
  --load \
  .
```

The only thing that changed from the first example is the Docker file.

Try the catalogue and cart features in the application

```shell
# Start the application in the background
docker run \
  --rm \
  --detach \
  --name 'application-monolithic-modular-single-project' \
  --publish 8080:8080 \
  'demo:application-monolithic-modular-single-project'

# Wait for the application to start
while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/cart/1')" -ne '200' ]; do echo 'Waiting for the application to start'; sleep 1; done
```

This starts our application in the background and waits until it is ready to
handle requests. The application is now running on localhost and listening on
port `8080`.

### Tradeoffs

The application is now organised by domain and provides clear boundaries between
different domains within the organisation. For the organisation to process and
handle orders it needs to introduce a payment and fulfilment component. All
payment related code will go to the *payment* package and the fulfilment related
code will go to the *fulfilment* package.

As the application grows, the team grows too and having everything in one
project may not be ideal. It is very easy to split this project into different
projects  now that it is organised by domain.

Please note that the cart still needs the catalogue as it depends on it.

> **Why would we split this into multiple projects?**
>
> There are many reasons why we would like to do that. Let’s consider the
> payments component. This component may require reviews by auditors before a
> new release could be released. Having all the code in one project means that
> every time the code is changed, then the whole project needs to be reviewed,
> even if the payment code is not changed.
>
> Furthermore, building and testing the whole application can be quite slow. I
> came across applications with millions of lines of code that take about an
> hour to build and test the whole application. This is quite slow, especially
> when working in an iterative approach.
>
> Moving the payment code into its own repository can mitigate these and other
> problems. Teams can be assigned to specific projects and only they can change
> the code while other teams may be able to open pull requests if needed. Each
> project can have their own build flow, which can be different based on the
> code. The shopping cart and the payment projects may have different
> requirements and a different workflow. In case of the payment project, an
> auditor may need to review and approve the code, for example, something that
> is not required by the shopping cart project.

> **Do you recommend one (big) code repository, or a repository per project?**
>
> There is more than meets the eye, here.
>
> Splitting the project into smaller projects does not also require moving each
> project into its own source code repository. An organisation can decide to put
> everything in one (big) repository. Google is famously known for this and they
> have a team of engineers looking after the huge (to say the least) repository
> and they have a set of tools that work with this repository.
>
> The one repository has several advantages. A refactor that affects multiple
> projects can happen in one commit. This can then trigger a build of the
> affected projects (not necessarily the whole thing) and then deployed. Note
> that in this case we still have one monolithic application that is deployed as
> a single application. Changing one project, or many projects, will always
> involve a new deployment of the whole application.
>
> Large repositories have their challenges too. Say that our projects involve
> thousands of classes with millions of lines of code, pulling the whole
> repository will take a long time and take a lot of space. Big companies have
> teams looking after large repositories and have created custom tools to help
> developers navigate it. Smaller organisations that do not have such bandwidth,
> should consider the implications of large repositories and consider smaller
> ones.
>
> The next option is to have a repository per team. A team may be responsible
> for several projects, all of which are found in the same repository. This
> allows the team to quickly refactor their code across projects as all are
> found in a single repository. This type of organisation finds a middle ground
> between large repositories and very small, one repository per project.
>
> Changes across repositories require coordination. Having code spread across
> multiple repositories makes it hard to find who is accessing what. Say a team
> needs to change one of their interfaces. They cannot look up the code and
> refactor both ends, not calculate the effort needed to make such a change.
> Additional tools may be needed to address these problems. It is important to
> avoid lockstep changes as this will undermine any benefits gained when
> splitting the project into smaller parts.

> **Are there any disadvantages when splitting the project into multiple projects?**
>
> Yes. There is no such thing as a free lunch.
>
> Let us put aside the challenges related to the multiple repositories, which
> was covered in the previous question.
>
> With one project, we have one built process that builds everything and then
> creates one artefact or a set of artefacts, usually in the form of JAR files,
> which are then deployed together. There is no need to make sure that the
> correct artefacts are being pulled as this is all generated during the build
> process.
>
> With multiple projects, and possible different build flows, there needs to be
> an assurance that the application works as expected once all the artefacts,
> usually in the form of JAR files, from all projects are pulled together. There
> is a chance that the wrong version is used which will cause the application to
> behave erroneously. These challenges are not present with one project and one
> build flow as all the code is built together.
>
> Like in many other aspects of software development and architecture,
> everything is a tradeoff, and we need to weigh the options and decide
> accordingly. Also note that what was viable a year ago, may not be anymore,
> and we need to re-evaluate our axioms as context changes.

#### Scoreboard

| Question                                                                                         | Score (1-5) |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------: |
| How quickly and easily can this application be deployed?                                         |             |
| How quickly and easily can features be added to the application?                                 |             |
| How safe does it feel to deploy changes without introducing new issues?                          |             |
| How quickly can issues be identified and resolved?                                               |             |
| How easy is it to implement a change to the application?                                         |             |
| How much effort is required to understand the system before changing it?                         |             |
| How satisfied are you when working on this project?                                              |             |
| How well does this architecture support collaboration and teamwork?                              |             |
| How well does this architecture position us to sustain or improve business/user goals over time? |             |

**Please do not proceed before submitting your scores**, as otherwise you may be
influenced by the scores shown here.

| Question                                                                                         | Weight | Layered Monolith | Modular Monolith | Motivation                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -----: | ---------------: | ---------------: | ----------------------------------------- |
| How quickly and easily can this application be deployed?                                         |      8 |                2 |                3 | One artifact, but modular boundaries help |
| How quickly and easily can features be added to the application?                                 |     10 |                2 |                4 | Domain partitioning localises changes     |
| How safe does it feel to deploy changes without introducing new issues?                          |      8 |                2 |                3 | Better modularity but still one deploy    |
| How quickly can issues be identified and resolved?                                               |      8 |                2 |                3 | Somewhat clearer module boundaries        |
| How easy is it to implement a change to the application?                                         |      6 |                2 |                4 | Domain focus helps flow                   |
| How much effort is required to understand the system before changing it?                         |      6 |                3 |                3 | Clearer domains but still one repo        |
| How satisfied are you when working on this project?                                              |      4 |                3 |                4 | Feels cleaner to work with                |
| How well does this architecture support collaboration and teamwork?                              |      4 |                2 |                4 | Modularity encourages domain ownership    |
| How well does this architecture position us to sustain or improve business/user goals over time? |      6 |                2 |                4 | Good balance of simplicity + modularity   |
| **This architecture style has a weighted score of**                                              |        |          **130** |          **210** |                                           |

This style partitions the system by business domains (cart, catalogue,
fulfilment), which directly improves lead time (4/5) and ease of change (4/5).
For example, adding a new promotion rule in the cart affects only the cart
module, with minimal impact on the catalogue or fulfilment. Because all modules
live in one repo and are deployed as a single artifact, deployment frequency
(3/5) is still constrained, but faster and safer than a layered monolith due to
better modular boundaries.

The change failure rate (3/5) is reduced compared with a layered monolith, since
changes are better isolated within modules. However, the system is still
deployed as one unit, so a failure in the cart could still roll back the
catalogue and fulfilment. MTTR (3/5) benefits slightly from clearer modular
logging, but the shared deployment package still complicates recovery.

From a developer perspective, cognitive load (3/5) is better managed because
domain boundaries reduce the need to understand unrelated parts of the code. A
fulfilment developer can focus mainly on fulfilment logic. This also improves
satisfaction (4/5) and team collaboration (4/5), as ownership aligns more
naturally with business areas. Overall, this architecture strikes a good balance
between simplicity and modularity, making it the strongest baseline for small to
medium applications.

#### Domain partitioning

Domain partitioning organises the code by the domain it belongs to.

```shell
tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 2 'src/main/java'
```

This command shows the top packages, which are

```
src/main/java
└── demo
    ├── cart
    ├── catalogue
    ├── common
    └── Main.java

5 directories, 1 file
```

By looking at the top-level packages, we can discern what this application is
about. The top-level package reflects the business language too. For instance,
if we want to add an image to the catalogue items, which package should we work
in? That’s not a tricky question - it’s the `demo.catalogue` package. Similarly,
if we need to allow the user to remove items from the shopping cart, where
should we look? Look no further than the `demo.cart` package.
